results.title: The winner takes it all – Effects of leaderboard-based feedback on cognitive performance and motivation - ScienceDirect
excerpts:
Even when only using individual game design elements in gamification, the effects of those elements might result in different levels of motivation and different behaviors, because most game design elements are adaptive and thus show different feedback and stimuli depending on the learners' behaviors. For example, point-based feedback ( Sailer & Sailer, 2021 ) or leaderboard-based feedback ( Bai et al., 2021 ; Nebel et al., 2016 ) can both result in differentiated feedback (e.g., positive or negative feedback) depending on user behavior (e.g., regarding engagement or cognitive performance). Such adaptivity of gamification was often neglected within prior research ( Ninaus & Nebel, 2021 ).

Leaderboards, which are among the most applied game design elements in gamification applications ( Zichermann & Cunningham, 2011 ), are particularly interesting in terms of the diverse information they provide adaptively to learners (see Bai et al., 2021 ).

...

Leaderboards can vary in their design, for example, by only providing learners with information about their direct neighbors on a leaderboard (relative leaderboard) or by providing learners with information about all or most of the competitors (absolute leaderboard; Zichermann & Cunningham, 2011 ). Bai et al. (2021) showed that the design features of leaderboards can influence how students experience the learning environment: In a relative leaderboard condition, students ranked in the top third tended to display better learning performance than their peers. In an absolute leaderboard condition, students at different positions showed similar levels of learning performance, but a higher position was associated with higher intrinsic motivation (see also Ninaus et al., 2020 ). Also, the difficulty of the underlying task matters, as shown by Cao et al.

...

The authors argue that thoughts of “what could have been” might have impacted the results (e.g., players in position four are about to enter the top three and might therefore be more willing to replay the game).

Overall, adaptive feedback regarding positions on leaderboards in gamified learning might indeed have a significant impact on learners, while general analyses of the effects of leaderboards (without applying a differentiated perspective) do not report similar effects. While higher-ranked learners tend to have more positive perceptions of the gamified environment, lower-ranked learners – or learners that barely miss out on a better position – report higher efforts to do better.

In summary, research on leaderboard effects suggests a relatively nuanced approach, considering, for example, design features (e.g., Bai et al., 2021 ), task difficulty (e.g., Cao et al., 2022 ), and the perception of individual positions (e.g., Bowey et al., 2015 ).
However, the perception of position shifts and differences between the perception of (starting) position and position shift have hardly been researched yet. Additionally, existing research has focused on approaches that utilize leaderboard-based feedback, reflecting learners' actual performance. Consequently, effects of leaderboard-based feedback on, for example, performance or motivation are usually not analyzed detached from learners' prior performance and, therefore, in a quasi-experimental way. More standardized ways of examining potential effects of leaderboard-based feedback could thus significantly enhance existing research by taking a more differentiated look at possible reasons behind previously found positive (or null) effects of leaderboards on motivation and performance.

### 1\.3. Theories about competition and leaderboards

...

Researchers often argue that leaderboards might provide a specific form of feedback to individual learners that can foster learners' experiences of competence ( Na & Han, 2023 ) and, thus, intrinsic motivation ( Mekler et al., 2017 ). However, this might only be true for higher-ranked learners ( Bowey et al., 2015 ). Contrarily, learners in lower positions might even tend to feel less competent ( Sailer & Sailer, 2021 ), while showing less interest ( Domínguez et al., 2013 ), based on the negative feedback they receive.

Social comparison theory ( Festinger, 1954 ) might help in interpreting such results: Leaderboards offer comparison categories for learners that vary depending on the actual position of learners. This might result in the application of different forms of comparisons (i.e., upward vs. downward comparison; Bai et al., 2021 ; Festinger, 1954 ).

...

Leaderboards and individual differences

Researchers also investigated individual differences and their potential role in gamified learning with leaderboards. Jia et al. (2017) , for example, investigated the Big-Five personality traits ( Goldberg, 1993 ) regarding their impact on the perceptions of leaderboards; however, they did not find substantial differences with respect to learners' motivation. Cao et al. (2022) investigated different goal orientations; however, the impact of low versus high task difficulty in a leaderboard learning condition was not moderated by learners' goal orientation (i.e., learning-orientation vs. performance-orientation; Dweck & Leggett, 1988 ). Amo et al. (2020) observed that while leaderboards enhanced engagement and performance among learners possessing high trait competitiveness, these same leaderboards tended to deter learners with low trait competitiveness.

...

Beyond that, the length of the study was relatively short and not focused on investigating long-lasting learning effects, meaning that we cannot make any predictions regarding potential long-term effects of implementing leaderboard-based feedback.

Second, the impact of competence frustration on motivation for players at different leaderboard positions can be examined in the future. Literature suggests that competence frustration, when administered properly, can help engage players more in games ( Abuhamdeh et al., 2015 ; Na & Han, 2023 ). Competence frustration occurs when individuals feel inadequate or experience failure ( Bartholomew et al., 2011 ). It arises from challenges perceived as too difficult, negative feedback, or situations in which their sense of mastery is undermined by personal criticism and social comparisons ( Ryan & Deci, 2017 ).

...

## Designing Leaderboards for Gamification: Perceived Differences Based on User Ranking, Application Domain, and Personality Traits

##### Files

Jia\_2018\_designing.pdf (1.65 MB) ##### Date

2017-05 ##### Authors

[Jia, Yuan](https://scholarworks.

...

Leaderboards, a common gamification technique, are used to enhance engagement through social comparisons. Prior research has demonstrated the overall utility of leaderboards but has not examined their effectiveness when individuals are ranked at particular levels or when the technique is applied in different application domains, such as social networking, fitness, or productivity. In this paper, we present a survey study investigating how preferences for leaderboards change based on individual differences (personality traits), ranking, social scoping, and application domains. Our results show that a respondent's position on the leaderboard had important effects on their perception of the leaderboard and the surrounding app, and that participants rated leaderboards most favorably in fitness apps and least favorably in social networking contexts. More extraverted people reported more positive experiences with leaderboards despite their ranking or the application domain.
We present design implications for creating leaderboards targeted at different domains and for different audiences. ##### Description ##### Keywords

## Abstract

Although fun is desirable in nearly all commercial games, defining it and actually getting it into a game can prove difficult.
Developers have added multiplayer features to their games since the beginning of the industry in an attempt to create fun, but to what extent does this actually affect a player's perception of a game's fun? This paper gives an overview of relevant research relating to fun and play before attempting to tackle the key issue of the effect of player success as measured by leaderboard rankings on the perception of a game's fun.

results.title: Effectively Design Leaderboard In Gamified Systems (Gamification)
excerpts:
Gamification is the integration of gaming dynamics into non-game contexts to leverage the motivational aspects inherent in games.

With a market valued at _$9.1 billion_ in 2020, it’s anticipated to reach _$30.7 billion_ by 2025. It aims to inject enthusiasm into routine tasks, enhancing engagement and performance across various sectors such as government services, work environments, crowdsourcing, commerce, health, education, environmental initiatives, marketing, and advertising.

Researchers are actively investigating the psychological mechanisms underlying gamification’s motivational effects.

Recent studies focus on dissecting individual gaming elements to understand their specific psychological functions, crucial for effective gamification design.

Among these elements, the **leaderboard** emerges as one of the most widely used and extensively researched components.

## What is a leaderboard?
It’s a popular tool in gamification, and serves to amplify engagement by facilitating social comparisons.

Leaderboards, a popular tool in gamification

They function as a ranking system, displaying the performance of players or teams and offering feedback on one’s standing compared to others. This fosters a competitive spirit, motivating users to enhance their performance as they compare themselves to peers.

Across various contexts, leaderboards have demonstrated positive outcomes. Previous research highlights their significance as one of the _most utilized game elements_ in gamification, effectively driving motivation through competition.

They are recognized as one of the _ten key ingredients in game design_ and one of the _seven primary game mechanics_ . Additionally, they feature prominently among the t _welve elements people appreciate_ in gamification, contributing to the overall enjoyment of a game.

...

While people acknowledge the leaderboard’s motivational impacts, such as _heightening user engagement, enhancing performance, and increasing participation_ , concerns have been raised regarding potential negative effects, with some studies suggesting that leader boards could become a _demotivating factor_ due to excessive competition.

Studies in digital gaming have explored how _players are motivated differently_ based on their leader board positions.

* Butler (2013) found that leaderboard ranks were not correlated with fun ratings , and lower-ranked players were more likely to replay the game.
* Sun et al. (2015) discovered that players in certain positions, such as 2nd, 4th, and 7th, reported higher satisfaction and enjoyment levels and were more inclined to replay and recommend the game.
* Bowey et al. (2015) revealed that higher-ranked players felt more competent, autonomous, and immersed in the game.

Gamification research has also focused on leader board positions.
* Jia et al. (2017) found that users generally preferred higher ranks, and motivation remained high even for those at the bottom of the leader board.
* Nebel et al. (2016) noted that lower-ranked learners exhibited higher competitive effort and better retention.
* Bai et al. (2021) discovered differences in motivation and engagement based on absolute and relative leader board studies.
* Codish and Ravid highlighted differences in how extraverted and introverted individuals perceive leader boards, while Jia et al. found that more extraverted individuals prefer leader boards in personal informatics systems.
* Additionally, a study on Olympic Games leader boards revealed that bronze medalists reported higher happiness levels than silver medalists.

Previous research has explored moderators of leader board effects, such as _personal development competitiveness_ and _trait competitiveness_ .
While some studies supported the influence of these moderators, others did not find significant effects.

Psychological mechanisms underlying leaderboard use include:

* Competition as a primary principle, goal-setting function, and the need for competence . According to Self-determination theory (SDT), _competence_ is a fundamental psychological need related to the desire for mastery and effectiveness in one’s environment.
* Unmet needs , as suggested by Sheldon and Gunz (2009), can also drive motivation and actions.
* Tillery and Fishbach (2014) proposed dimensions of motivation , including outcome-focused and process-focused motivation, which can indicate intrinsic or extrinsic motivation.

## Practical implications for designing leaderboards

Derived from gamification research, encompass several key considerations:

### 1\. Domain-Specific Design

Tailor leaderboards to suit the domain where they will be implemented.
In social networking contexts, leaderboards should prioritize _facilitating communication_ among friends rather than solely emphasizing competition. For instance, showcasing long-time, no-contact friends or shared-interest strangers may enhance engagement more effectively than focusing solely on performance metrics within stable friend groups.

Similarly, in fitness applications, leaderboards can introduce an _element of playfulness_ , encouraging participants to increase physical activity.

Workplace leaderboards should be implemented cautiously, as they can either improve punctuality or reduce performance depending on their visibility and impact on employees’ perceptions.

### 2\. Fairness in Competition

Ensure that the competitive activities used to seed leaderboards promote a sense of fairness among users.

Consider individual personality differences, as extraverts may perceive leaderboards differently in various contexts.

### 3\. Participant Relationships
Prioritize understanding the relationships among participants before determining leaderboard positioning.

Focus on _supporting constructive competition_ within small circles of friends or colleagues, as this can motivate individuals to improve performance, particularly in areas like fitness where personal decisions may affect others’ perceptions.

### 4\. Placement Considerations

Carefully consider where active users should be displayed on leaderboards, taking into account the domain and user preferences.

In productivity-oriented contexts, respondents typically prefer seeing their names among the top entries, while appearing at the bottom can lead to negative perceptions and potential strain on relationships.

Designers should select competitive tasks that are simple and repetitive to maintain engagement and avoid demotivating effects.

### 5\. Dynamic Competitive Landscape
Extraverted individuals tend to have more positive perceptions of leaderboards due to their dynamic nature, reflecting changes in the social landscape of the gamified system’s participants. Designers should highlight these changes to appeal to extraverted users effectively.

In summary, designing effective leaderboards requires careful consideration of the specific domain, fairness in competition, participant relationships, placement strategies, and the dynamic nature of the competitive landscape. By addressing these factors, designers can create leaderboards that motivate users and enhance engagement ac
